section_1.title: Intuitive Prerequisite: Antipodal Points
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a sphere and antipodal points (points directly opposite each other, like the North and South Poles). Visualize this as a sphere in 3D space, mapping points x and -x.
section_1.example: Imagine a balloon with a temperature sensor at every point. The Borsuk-Ulam theorem guarantees that at any moment, there exist two opposite points on the balloon with identical temperature.

section_2.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem (Formalized)
section_2.content: Define the theorem: Any continuous function from an n-dimensional sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space maps at least one pair of antipodal points to the same value. Use a 2D circle mapping to a 1D line as a visual simplification.
section_2.example: A visual animation showing a circle being 'folded' onto a line; the animation highlights two points that inevitably land on the same spot on the line.

section_3.title: The Stolen Necklace Problem
section_3.content: Transition to the application: Two thieves steal a necklace containing beads of different types (e.g., gold and silver). The necklace must be cut into pieces and distributed such that both thieves get an equal number of each bead type, with the minimum number of cuts.
section_3.example: An animation of a necklace with 10 gold beads and 10 silver beads. A 'cut' acts as a partition. We demonstrate how the Borsuk-Ulam theorem provides the non-constructive proof that it is always possible.

section_4.title: Bridging Theory to Practice
section_4.content: Explain the connection: The necklace configuration space is a high-dimensional sphere. The distribution of beads represents the continuous mapping. The 'cut' points represent the points on the sphere being evaluated.
section_4.example: A graphic showing the necklace being mapped onto a high-dimensional geometric space where the 'equal division' is the intersection point predicted by the theorem.

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Summarize how abstract topology solves concrete discrete problems. Emphasize that while the theorem proves it's possible, it doesn't always tell us where to cut, highlighting the elegance of non-constructive mathematical existence proofs.
section_5.example: A final visual of two happy characters (thieves) holding their fair share of beads, with a concluding thought: 'Topology isn't just shapes—it's a tool for perfect fairness.'

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text("- " + line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Visualize a sphere in 3D space.",
            "Identify points directly opposite each other.",
            "These are called antipodal points.",
            "Example: North and South Poles.",
            "They share identical properties."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Intuitive Prerequisite: Antipodal Points", lecture_lines)
        
        # Elements
        sphere = Sphere(radius=1.2, fill_opacity=0.3, color=BLUE)
        axes = ThreeDAxes(x_range=[-2, 2], y_range=[-2, 2], z_range=[-2, 2], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        
        p_north = sphere.get_top()
        p_south = sphere.get_bottom()
        
        dot_n = Dot(p_north, color=YELLOW)
        dot_s = Dot(p_south, color=RED)
        
        label_n = Text("N", font_size=20, color=YELLOW).next_to(dot_n, UP, buff=0.1)
        label_s = Text("S", font_size=20, color=RED).next_to(dot_s, DOWN, buff=0.1)
        
        # Group sphere and axes
        scene_group = VGroup(axes, sphere, dot_n, dot_s, label_n, label_s)
        self.place_in_area(scene_group, 'A1', 'F6', scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.play(Create(axes), Create(sphere))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        self.play(FadeIn(dot_n), FadeIn(dot_s))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(ORANGE))
        self.play(Write(label_n), Write(label_s))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(RED))
        self.play(Indicate(dot_n), Indicate(dot_s))
        self.wait(1)
